item.text: {"question_id":"4B.4","answer":"During 2023, courts, the electoral commission, auditors, and human-rights monitors retained some formal or operational checking capacity, but the supplied evidence does not establish that Tshisekedi consistently protected their independence when they could constrain him. The Constitutional Court validated 26 presidential candidacies and reinstated two candidates; CENI published terms for an external voter-register audit requiring mixed national/international expertise, conflict-of-interest exclusions, assessment of inclusiveness and accuracy, publication of results, and possible legal action. CENI also announced selected auditors and reported that a five-member mixed expert team found the register reliable, subject to recommendations. These are institutional safeguards and review mechanisms, but the sources do not establish presidential non-interference, audit independence in practice, full implementation, or effective follow-up. [BATCH-0005-E005, BATCH-0027-E011, BATCH-0027-E001, BATCH-0023-E015] Formal judicial rules and the 2023 Superior Council of the Court of Auditors procedure were recorded, and Tshisekedi publicly endorsed ICC cooperation and the rule of law. The National Commission on Human Rights issued reports, visited detention centers, trained magistrates, and followed complaints; however, authorities denied UN access to some military and intelligence detention sites, the commission lacked full-time representation in all provinces, and observers described it as somewhat independent but ineffective. [BATCH-0016-E010, BATCH-0019-E001, BATCH-0011-E014] Against this, presidential ordinances revoked, compulsorily retired, reassigned, promoted, and appointed civilian and military judges and prosecutors, including senior officials; the supplied records give no individual reasons, selection criteria, qualifications, or evidence of subsequent independence. The presidency presented these changes as judicial reform, but that stated rationale is not independent proof of protection. [BATCH-0015-E006, BATCH-0019-E006, BATCH-0019-E007] Tshisekedi's state of siege replaced elected provincial governors and assemblies in Nord-Kivu and Ituri with military administration and authorized military courts to prosecute civilians; Amnesty described the repeated extensions as unlawful and lacking meaningful public debate, while the precise parliamentary role in each extension is not supplied. [BATCH-0012-R03-E003] Election observers and later assessments reported unexplained or insufficiently reasoned court decisions, suspected corruption involving electoral judges, politicization concerns regarding CENI and the Constitutional Court, nontransparent tabulation, and opposition reluctance to appeal because courts were viewed as controlled by Tshisekedi. These findings concern institutions under his administration but do not by themselves prove a personal order or unlawful interference. [BATCH-0001-E016, BATCH-0008-E004, BATCH-0013-E009, BATCH-0028-E017, BATCH-0028-E018, BATCH-0028-E023] Tshisekedi stated that he would not intervene in journalist Stanis Bujakera's case, invoking separation of powers; that supports a stated non-intervention position but does not establish fair adjudication or institutional independence. [BATCH-0025-E013] Later parliamentary and Court of Accounts scrutiny of 2023 budget execution shows that oversight bodies could criticize government spending, provincial allocations, and alleged financial irregularities, but it occurred in 2024 and therefore does not demonstrate that Tshisekedi protected those bodies during the 2023 target period; nor does it establish their funding or local-government autonomy. [BATCH-0024-E003, BATCH-0024-E004] Overall, the evidence supports formal capacity and some institutional review, alongside material ruler-attributed personnel intervention and executive substitution of elected provincial authority, but not reliable protection of jurisdiction, appointment independence, tenure, funding, local-government autonomy, or decisions constraining the executive.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0005-E005","BATCH-0027-E011","BATCH-0027-E001","BATCH-0023-E015","BATCH-0016-E010","BATCH-0019-E001","BATCH-0011-E014","BATCH-0015-E006","BATCH-0019-E006","BATCH-0019-E007","BATCH-0012-R03-E003","BATCH-0025-E013"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0001-E016","BATCH-0008-E004","BATCH-0013-E009","BATCH-0028-E017","BATCH-0028-E018","BATCH-0028-E023","BATCH-0024-E003","BATCH-0024-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The supplied evidence does not establish the reasons, criteria, qualifications, tenure effects, or later independence of judicial appointees and removals.","Presidential non-interference in CENI, the Constitutional Court, auditors, and the National Commission on Human Rights is not established.","The CENI audit's practical independence, complete findings, publication, and implementation of recommendations remain unresolved.","The state-of-siege legal text and parliamentary involvement in each extension are incompletely documented.","Legislative independence, institutional funding, and local-government autonomy are not directly documented.","The later budget-account review is retrospective and cannot establish target-period protection of oversight institutions.","Perceptions of politicization, opposition reluctance to litigate, and institutional dysfunction do not alone prove unlawful personal presidential interference.","The supplied evidence concerns 2023 and limited retrospective early-2024 reporting; it does not establish the full duration or trajectory of institutional effects."] ,"corrections_made":["Added the omitted evidence on prosecutorial and Constitutional Court appointments, the Court of Auditors' procedure rules, CENI audit terms, auditor selection, conflict-of-interest safeguards, and National Commission on Human Rights monitoring and access limitations.","Reweighted the later parliamentary and Court of Accounts material as post-period evidence of institutional scrutiny rather than proof of target-period protection.","Made the distinction between formal institutional capacity, institutional conduct, and direct Tshisekedi attribution explicit.","Preserved favorable, adverse, mixed, and uncertain evidence without converting the answer into a score."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["A full review would be warranted if the underlying judicial ordinances, audit report, audit implementation record, state-of-siege extension records, budget-review documents, or evidence on legislative and local-government autonomy become available."]}
